<p class="lx-eyebrow">A 300 MW load on the Plains Grid, 7 November 2025: four questions, four answers</p>
<table class="lx-facts a10-fb">
<thead><tr><th scope="col">Question</th><th scope="col">Data center (7,200 MWh)</th><th scope="col">Electrolyzer (3,600 MWh)</th></tr></thead>
<tbody>
<tr><td>1 · Inventory share, at average factors</td><td data-label="Data center">1,611 t</td><td data-label="Electrolyzer">553 t</td></tr>
<tr><td>2 · Short-run change at the plants</td><td data-label="Data center">+3,039 t</td><td data-label="Electrolyzer">+1,435 t</td></tr>
<tr><td>2 · The same, with a must-run rule</td><td data-label="Data center">+2,211 t</td><td data-label="Electrolyzer">+607 t</td></tr>
<tr><td>3 · Long run, a new 300 MW gas plant</td><td data-label="Data center">+2,372 t</td><td data-label="Electrolyzer">+934 t</td></tr>
<tr><td>3 · Long run, new wind for its yearly energy</td><td data-label="Data center">+133 t</td><td data-label="Electrolyzer">+24 t</td></tr>
<tr><td>4 · Claim, certificates matched over the year</td><td data-label="Data center">0 t</td><td data-label="Electrolyzer">0 t</td></tr>
<tr><td>4 · Claim, new wind matched hour by hour (short hours at the grid average, a proxy)</td><td data-label="Data center">441 t</td><td data-label="Electrolyzer">137 t</td></tr>
</tbody>
</table>
<p class="lx-hint">Claims follow illustrative rules after the GHG Protocol's Scope 2 Guidance (2015): certificates are assumed to be the buyer's alone, retired for it and from the same market.</p>
<p class="lx-hint">New wind is assumed to be built for the buyer (additional) and to reach this grid (deliverable).</p>
<p class="lx-hint">The electrolyzer runs from 00:00 to 12:00, the 12 hours with the lowest average factor (0.10 to 0.17 t CO₂ per MWh). Each of its extra MWh is still served by the combined-cycle plants, at 0.40 t.</p>
<p class="lx-hint">With JavaScript on, you pick the load, switch the model's rule, choose what gets built and compare five purchases.</p>
</div>
</div>
<p class="lx-datanote"><svg class="lx-ic" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8" aria-hidden="true"><circle cx="12" cy="12" r="8.5"/><path d="M12 11v5M12 8v.2"/></svg><span><b>Illustrative grid.</b> The Plains Grid is fictional: a 4,000 MW peak; 3,000 MW of wind, 600 MW of solar, 2,000 MW of gas combined-cycle plants and 2,300 MW of gas peakers.</span></p>
<p class="lx-datanote"><svg class="lx-ic" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8" aria-hidden="true"><circle cx="12" cy="12" r="8.5"/><path d="M12 11v5M12 8v.2"/></svg><span><b>Real plant data.</b> Gas plants' full-load <span class="lx-term" data-term="heat-rate">heat rates</span> are 7,535 and 10,975 Btu per kWh (<a href="https://www.eia.gov/electricity/annual/html/epa_08_02.html">EIA, 2025</a>), held at every output; gas emits 52.91 kg CO₂ per MMBtu (<a href="https://www.eia.gov/environment/emissions/co2_vol_mass.php">EIA</a>).</span></p>
<p class="lx-datanote"><svg class="lx-ic" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8" aria-hidden="true"><circle cx="12" cy="12" r="8.5"/><path d="M12 11v5M12 8v.2"/></svg><span><b>From heat to CO₂.</b> 7,535 Btu per kWh = 7.535 <span class="lx-term" data-term="mmbtu">MMBtu</span> per MWh; × 52.91 kg = 399 kg. So 0.40 and 0.58 t per MWh, counted at the stack; t is a metric tonne, 1,000 kg.</span></p>
<p class="lx-datanote"><svg class="lx-ic" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8" aria-hidden="true"><circle cx="12" cy="12" r="8.5"/><path d="M12 11v5M12 8v.2"/></svg><span><b>Real hours.</b> Demand, wind and sun follow the Southwest Power Pool's hours of 7 November 2025 (<a href="https://www.eia.gov/electricity/gridmonitor/">EIA-930</a>), wind and sun scaled to EIA's 2025 capacity factors (<a href="https://www.eia.gov/electricity/monthly/epm_table_grapher.php?t=epmt_6_07_b">Table 6.07.B</a>). Each hour runs cheapest first, with no ramp limits.</span></p>
<p class="lx-hint" style="margin-top:.6rem">About 30 guided minutes in seven steps.</p>

::: {#explain .lx-sec}
::: {.lx-sec-h}
## What you just did, as diagrams
:::

```{=html}
<div id="a10-explain" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<dl class="lx-ideas">
<dt>Inventory</dt><dd>Average factors share a total that already happened: the data center's 1,611 t and everyone else's 12,055 t add up to the grid's 13,666 t.</dd>
<dt>Short run</dt><dd>Marginal factors ask what changes: the data center adds 3,039 t, mostly at the combined-cycle plants.</dd>
<dt>The model matters</dt><dd>With a rule that keeps 800 MW of combined-cycle plants running, night wind would be spilled, and the electrolyzer's change falls from 1,435 t to 607 t.</dd>
<dt>Long run</dt><dd>What gets built decides the answer: +2,372 t with a new gas plant, +133 t with new wind, for the data center that day.</dd>
<dt>Claim</dt><dd>A purchase sets what may be reported under a stated rule. In these scenarios the plants change only when we assume it adds clean power that reaches this grid.</dd>
</dl>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>Two ways to report electricity's CO₂</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

- **[Scope 2]{.lx-term term="scope-2"}.** A company's reported emissions from the electricity, heat or steam it buys. Where buyers can choose contracts, the GHG Protocol's Scope 2 Guidance (2015) asks for two counts.
- **[Location-based]{.lx-term term="location-based"}.** Each MWh is counted at the grid's average factor where it is used: question 1.
- **[Market-based]{.lx-term term="market-based"}.** Each MWh is counted at the factor of the electricity the buyer purchased, through contracts or certificates: question 4.
- **Conditions.** Among other criteria, a certificate must be the buyer's alone, retired for it and from the same market (Table 7.1). Unclaimed use takes a [residual mix]{.lx-term term="residual-mix"}; this lesson uses the grid average instead, as a proxy.
- **Rules under review.** The GHG Protocol consulted on a revision from 20 October 2025 to 31 January 2026. Hourly matching and deliverability are proposals, not adopted rules; its summary of 29 July 2026 reports low support for them as proposed.
- **Neither method** measures what the plants do differently: that is questions 2 and 3.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>Where marginal factors come from</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

- **From a dispatch model.** Solve the hour with and without one more MWh; the change in CO₂ is the hour's marginal factor under that model's rules (fuel prices, minimum outputs, lines).
- **From statistics.** Regress the hourly change in a region's CO₂ on the change in its generation over years of data (Siler-Evans et al., 2012).
- **Long run.** A planning model adds the load and compares the build-out with and without it (Gagnon and Cole, 2022).
- **Next.** [M6](m06-carbon-in-models.html) puts carbon and a matching rule into such a planning model.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper</span>What this lesson leaves out</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li>A year: one windy November day stands for no other day.</li>
<li>Life-cycle emissions: building plants, and methane leaks before the gas reaches the plant.</li>
<li>Imports, exports and the lines inside the grid: its plants serve its load from one point.</li>
<li>Start-ups, ramp limits and reserves, which change which plant responds.</li>
<li>Part-load efficiency: each plant burns its full-load fuel per MWh at every output.</li>
</ul>
</div>
</details>
</div>
```
:::

## Check yourself
:::

```{=html}
<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="a10-myth">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="clean-hours" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “The hours with the lowest average CO₂ factor are the hours when extra use adds the least CO₂.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth, here. From 00:00 to 12:00 the average is 0.10 to 0.17 t per MWh, yet each extra MWh comes from the combined-cycle plants at 0.40 t.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="certificates" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “When a buyer may claim zero emissions, its use adds no CO₂ at the plants.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. With certificates from an existing wind farm the data center may claim 0 t, while the plants emit 3,039 t more that day: the purchase added nothing to the grid.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="add-up" data-answer="fact">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Inventory shares of every user add up to the grid's total; marginal changes need not.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Fact. Shares divide a total that happened. A marginal change answers a different question: what one user's choice changes.</p></details>
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-quiz" data-quiz="a10">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="share" data-answer="b">
<p class="lx-qtext">In one hour the plants emit 2,000 t of CO₂ for 8,000 MWh of use. A load uses 100 MWh in that hour. What is its inventory share?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">2,000 t</li><li data-value="b">25 t</li><li data-value="c">40 t</li><li data-value="d">0.25 t</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>25 t: the average factor is 2,000 ÷ 8,000 = 0.25 t per MWh, times 100 MWh.</p><p>40 t would be the 0.40 t of a combined-cycle plant on the margin: question 2, not question 1.</p></details>
</div>
</div>
```

<blockquote class="lx-excerpt" data-source="excerpt:ghg"><p>In the reported scenarios, reductions in attributed emissions were on the order of one to two percent of regional totals or less.</p><p>Reductions are computed under average-emission-intensity accounting with perfect foresight; they are not estimates of the consequential (marginal) system response.</p><footer>Approved excerpt of: Li et al. (2025), <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.crsus.2025.100367">Cell Reports Sustainability</a>.</footer></blockquote>

<blockquote class="lx-excerpt" data-source="excerpt:txh2"><p>When gas-fired backup power became much more expensive, the model built fuel cells and turned stored green hydrogen back into electricity.</p><p>Industry then drew more hydrogen from gas reformers, and the round trip from power to hydrogen and back lost energy, so total emissions rose although gas-plant emissions fell.</p><footer>Approved excerpt of: Li et al. (2025), <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijhydene.2025.02.303">International Journal of Hydrogen Energy</a>.</footer></blockquote>
